quiz.explain: 15 hours is 3 half-lives, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 remains.

quiz.prompt: Solve for x: 3^x = 81.
Which single logarithm equals log(a) + log(b), taken to the same base?
quiz.answer: log(ab)
quiz.explain: Adding logarithms multiplies the arguments, because exponents add when powers are multiplied.

quiz.prompt: A colony of bacteria grows by 8% every hour. Roughly how long does it take to double?
quiz.answer: About 9 hours
quiz.explain: Doubling takes log(2)/log(1.08), about 9 hours. Dividing 100 by 8 ignores compounding and overshoots.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate log base 10 of 1000000.
quiz.explain: A logarithm asks what exponent produces the number, and 10^6 = 1000000. Counting the zeros gives base-10 logs of round numbers instantly.

quiz.prompt: A car worth $20000 loses 20% of its value each year. What is it worth after two years?
quiz.explain: Each year the value is multiplied by 0.8, so after two years it is 20000 x 0.64 = $12,800. Subtracting 40% in one go would wrongly treat the decay as linear.

quiz.prompt: Which single logarithm equals log(a) - log(b), taken to the same base?
quiz.answer: log(a/b)
quiz.explain: Logarithms turn division of the inputs into subtraction of the outputs, so the difference collapses to log(a/b). Subtracting logs is not the log of a difference.

quiz.prompt: Solve for x: 2^(x + 1) = 16.
quiz.explain: Since 16 = 2^4, the exponents match: x + 1 = 4, so x = 3. Rewriting both sides with a common base turns an exponential equation into a linear one.

lesson_media.alt: The graphs of two to the x and log base two of x reflect across y equals x; the ordered point (3, 8) becomes (8, 3).
lesson_media.caption: A logarithm returns the exponent, so it reverses exponentiation.

nodes.title: Sequences and Series
nodes.goal: Arithmetic and geometric patterns, sums to infinity.

quiz.prompt: An arithmetic sequence begins 4, 7, 10, ... What is its 10th term?
quiz.explain: With first term 4 and common difference 3, the 10th term is 4 + 9 x 3 = 31.

quiz.prompt: A geometric series has first term 1 and common ratio one half. What value do its partial sums approach?
quiz.explain: For a ratio smaller than 1 in size the sum is a/(1 - r) = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2, which the partial sums 1, 1.5, 1.75, ... creep toward.

quiz.prompt: A geometric sequence begins 3, 6, 12, ... What is its 6th term?
quiz.explain: With first term 3 and ratio 2, the 6th term is 3 x 2^5 = 96.

quiz.prompt: An arithmetic series has first term 5 and common difference 4. What is the sum of its first 10 terms?
quiz.explain: The 10th term is 5 + 9 x 4 = 41, and the sum is 10 x (5 + 41) / 2 = 230.

quiz.prompt: For which common ratio does an infinite geometric series fail to settle on a finite total?
quiz.explain: Convergence needs the ratio to be smaller than 1 in size. With r = 1.5 the terms grow, so the partial sums run away.

quiz.prompt: A sequence is defined by a(1) = 2 and a(n + 1) = 3a(n) - 1. What is a(4)?
quiz.explain: The terms run 2, 5, 14, 41: each one is tripled and then reduced by 1.

quiz.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has 5th term 17 and 9th term 33. What is its common difference?
quiz.explain: Four steps carry you from the 5th term to the 9th, a rise of 16, so each step is 4. In an arithmetic sequence the difference between terms is constant.

quiz.prompt: An infinite geometric series has first term 6 and common ratio one third. What is its sum?
quiz.explain: The sum is a/(1 - r) = 6/(2/3) = 9. The formula applies because the ratio has absolute value below 1, so the terms shrink fast enough to settle.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a geometric sequence?
quiz.explain: Each term of 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before, a constant ratio. A constant difference, as in 2, 6, 10, 14, makes a sequence arithmetic instead.

quiz.prompt: A ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 60% of its previous height on each bounce. What happens to the total vertical distance it travels?
quiz.answer: The total approaches a finite limit
choices: The total approaches a finite limit
The total grows beyond any bound
The total stays fixed at 2 m
The total doubles with each bounce
quiz.explain: The bounce heights form a geometric sequence with ratio 0.6, and a geometric series with ratio below 1 converges. Infinitely many bounces still add to a finite distance.

lesson_media.alt: Successively smaller geometric terms fill a bar toward, but not past, a total of two.
lesson_media.caption: An infinite geometric series converges only when the ratio's absolute value is below one.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.goal: Count outcomes; compute chances.

quiz.prompt: You roll one fair six-sided die. What is the probability of getting an even number?
quiz.explain: Three of the six outcomes (2, 4, 6) are even, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

quiz.prompt: You flip two fair coins. What is the probability of getting two heads? Give a decimal.
quiz.explain: Each coin shows heads with probability 1/2, so both do with probability 1/2 x 1/2 = 0.25.

quiz.prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You draw two marbles without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
quiz.explain: P(first red) x P(second red) = (3/5) x (2/4) = 6/20 = 3/10.

quiz.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, how many give a total of 7?
quiz.explain: The pairs are 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1, so 6 of the 36 outcomes total 7.

quiz.prompt: A disease affects 1 person in 10000. A test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. Someone tests positive. Roughly what is the chance they have the disease?
quiz.answer: About 1%
quiz.explain: Among 10000 people, about 1 true case tests positive but about 100 healthy people do too, so a positive result is right roughly 1 time in 100.

quiz.prompt: You flip a fair coin five times and get five heads. What is the probability that the next flip is heads?
quiz.answer: Exactly 1/2, as on any single flip
choices: Exactly 1/2, as on any single flip
quiz.explain: Coins have no memory, so the run leaves the next flip at 1/2; 1/32 is the chance of five heads before any flipping starts.

quiz.prompt: Three fair coins are flipped. How many of the eight equally likely outcomes show exactly two heads?
quiz.explain: The outcomes HHT, HTH and THH each show two heads, so 3 of the 8. Listing outcomes systematically avoids double counting.

quiz.prompt: A spinner has 8 equal sectors, 3 of them red. What is the probability of landing somewhere other than red?
quiz.explain: Five of the eight sectors are not red, so the probability is 5/8. Equivalently, take 1 minus the probability of red, the complement rule.

quiz.prompt: You draw a card, put it back, shuffle, and draw again. Compared with drawing twice without putting the first card back, what changes?
quiz.answer: The two draws become independent
choices: The two draws become mutually exclusive
The second draw becomes likelier to match the first
The number of possible outcomes shrinks
quiz.explain: Replacing the card restores the deck, so the first result leaves the second unaffected: the draws are independent. Without replacement the second probability depends on what was removed.

quiz.prompt: A machine part fails with probability 0.1, and two such parts behave independently. What is the probability that at least one of them fails?
quiz.explain: Both survive with probability 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81, so at least one fails with probability 1 - 0.81 = 0.19. Simply adding the two failure chances double counts the case where both fail.

lesson_media.alt: A two-draw tree shows how removing the first marble changes the second probability.
lesson_media.caption: Without replacement, later chances depend on earlier outcomes; replacement restores independence.

nodes.title: Statistics
nodes.goal: Describe data, spot spread, question claims.

quiz.prompt: For the data set 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, which statement is true?
quiz.answer: The mode is 4
quiz.explain: 4 appears most often; the mean is 5, the median is 4.5, and the range is 7.

quiz.prompt: Which of these data sets has the largest standard deviation?
quiz.explain: Standard deviation measures how far the values sit from their mean. The first set has mean 10 with deviations of 8, 2, 2 and 8; the second has mean 10 with deviations of 5 throughout, and the last two barely move at all.

quiz.prompt: A town reports that mean income rose from $40,000 to $44,000 last year while median income fell from $35,000 to $34,000. Which account fits both figures?
quiz.answer: A few top earners gained a lot while most incomes slipped
quiz.explain: The mean follows the total, so a handful of very large rises can lift it; the median follows the household in the middle, and it went down. Both figures can be right at once, so no arithmetic error is needed to explain them. A rise shared by nearly everyone would have carried the median up too, and extra households of ordinary income would pull the mean toward the middle rather than above it.
choices: Nearly every household's income rose by about a tenth
One of the two figures must have been computed wrongly
A few top earners gained a lot while most incomes slipped
More people moved to the town, which lifts any average

quiz.prompt: A data set contains the values 4, 4, 6 and 10. Treating these four as the whole population, what is the variance?
quiz.explain: The mean is 6, the squared deviations are 4, 4, 0 and 16, and their average is 24 / 4 = 6.

quiz.prompt: A city reports a mean commute of 32 minutes and a median of 24 minutes. Give one distribution shape that is consistent with this gap, without claiming the two summaries prove that shape.
quiz.answer: A right-skewed distribution is consistent with the figures: a tail of long commutes could pull the mean above the median, although the summaries alone do not determine the full shape.
quiz.explain: A right-hand tail is a common explanation for mean above median, but two summary values do not uniquely determine a distribution's shape. A plot or the underlying data is needed to establish the shape.

quiz.prompt: Two towns have the same mean annual temperature, but town A has a much larger standard deviation. What follows?
quiz.answer: Town A's temperatures are more dispersed around their mean
choices: Town A has a higher median
Town A has more days above the mean than below it
Town A's temperatures are more dispersed around their mean
quiz.explain: Standard deviation measures aggregate spread around the mean rather than its level. A larger value does not by itself prove that town A has extremes on both sides, a higher median, or more days above the mean; those depend on the distribution's shape.

quiz.prompt: The values 3, 7, 8, 12, 15, 19 are already in order. What is the median?
quiz.explain: With an even count the median is the mean of the two middle values, (8 + 12)/2 = 10. The median need not be one of the data values.

quiz.prompt: A class of 20 students has a mean score of 70. One more student joins with a score of 91. What happens to the mean?
quiz.answer: It rises to 71
quiz.explain: The total was 1400; adding 91 gives 1491 over 21 students, which is exactly 71. Averaging the old mean with the new score ignores how many students each represents.

quiz.prompt: A newspaper invites readers to vote on its website and reports that 80% back a new policy. Why should you treat that figure carefully?
quiz.answer: Readers who choose to respond are not a random sample
choices: Readers who choose to respond are not a random sample
Percentages are the wrong way to report a vote
A sample of that size is too small to report
The median would have been the better summary
quiz.explain: Self-selected respondents tend to be the people who feel strongly, so the sample is biased regardless of its size. How a sample is chosen matters more than how large it is.

quiz.prompt: Ice cream sales and drownings both climb in July, and a report concludes that ice cream causes drownings. What is wrong with the reasoning?
quiz.answer: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
choices: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
The data covered a single month
Drownings cause the ice cream sales instead
quiz.explain: Two variables can move together because a common cause pushes both, so correlation is not evidence of causation. Here warm days send people to both the freezer and the water.

lesson_media.alt: Two distributions share a mean, but one has values much farther from it and a larger standard deviation.
lesson_media.caption: Centre and spread describe different features; neither alone tells the whole distribution.

nodes.title: Vectors
nodes.goal: Quantities with direction: add, scale, dot.

quiz.prompt: What is the magnitude of the vector (3, 4)?
quiz.explain: Magnitude = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.

quiz.prompt: Compute the dot product of (2, 3) and (4, -1).
quiz.explain: Dot product = 2 x 4 + 3 x (-1) = 8 - 3 = 5.
Add componentwise: (1 + 3, 2 + (-5)) = (4, -3).

quiz.prompt: A vector has magnitude 10 and makes an angle of 60 degrees with the positive x-axis. What is its x-component?
quiz.explain: The x-component is 10 cos(60) = 10 x 0.5 = 5.

quiz.prompt: Two nonzero vectors have a dot product of zero. What does that tell you about them?
quiz.answer: They are perpendicular
choices: One runs along the x-axis and the other along the y-axis
quiz.explain: The dot product is |a||b|cos(theta), which vanishes when cos(theta) = 0, that is at 90 degrees. Parallel vectors give the largest positive value and opposite vectors the largest negative one. Lying along the two axes is only one way to be perpendicular: (3, 4) and (-4, 3) manage it without either one following an axis.

quiz.prompt: A boat heads due north at 8 km/h while the current carries it due east at 6 km/h. What is its speed over the ground?
quiz.answer: 10 km/h
quiz.explain: The two velocities are perpendicular, so the resultant has magnitude sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = 10 km/h; they do not simply add.

quiz.prompt: What is the magnitude of the vector (-6, 8)?
quiz.explain: Magnitude is the square root of 36 + 64 = 100, which is 10. Negative components square to positive numbers, so direction does not shrink the length.
Scaling gives (6, -3), and subtracting (4, 2) componentwise gives (2, -5). Scalar multiplication touches both components.

quiz.prompt: The dot product of two nonzero vectors comes out negative. What does that say about the angle between them?
quiz.answer: It is larger than 90 degrees
quiz.explain: The dot product equals |a||b|cos(theta), and cosine is negative for angles between 90 and 180 degrees. A zero dot product would mean a right angle.

quiz.prompt: A plane flies north at 300 km/h while the wind blows south at 40 km/h. What is its speed over the ground?
quiz.answer: 260 km/h
quiz.explain: The two vectors point along the same line in opposite directions, so the magnitudes subtract to give 260 km/h. The Pythagorean combination applies only when the vectors are perpendicular.

lesson_media.alt: Perpendicular north and east velocity vectors combine into a ten-unit diagonal resultant.
lesson_media.caption: Vectors add component by component; direction determines whether magnitudes combine, cancel, or form a right triangle.

nodes.title: Limits: a First Look
nodes.goal: What functions approach — the gateway to calculus.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the limit of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) as x approaches 2.
quiz.explain: Factor the numerator as (x - 2)(x + 2), cancel (x - 2), and evaluate x + 2 at x = 2 to get 4.

quiz.prompt: What is the limit of 1/x as x approaches infinity?
quiz.explain: As x grows without bound, 1/x shrinks toward 0.

quiz.prompt: The function f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) has a hole in its graph at x = 1. Which statement describes what happens there?
quiz.answer: The limit exists and equals 2, though f(1) is undefined
choices: The limit exists and equals 2, though f(1) is undefined
The limit fails to exist because f(1) is undefined
The limit equals 1, the value x is approaching
The graph jumps from one value to another
quiz.explain: Away from x = 1 the function equals x + 1, which approaches 2. A limit describes the approach, not the value at the point.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the limit of (3x^2 + 5x)/(x^2 - 2) as x grows without bound.
quiz.explain: Divide top and bottom by x^2 to get (3 + 5/x)/(1 - 2/x^2); the small terms vanish, leaving 3.

quiz.prompt: With x measured in radians, what is the limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches 0?
quiz.explain: With angles in radians, sin(x) and x are asymptotically equal near zero, so the ratio approaches 1 even though the expression is undefined at the point.

quiz.prompt: At x = 2 a function has a left-hand limit of 3 and a right-hand limit of 5. What can you say about the limit at x = 2?
quiz.answer: It does not exist
choices: It equals 4, the average of the two
quiz.explain: A two-sided limit exists when both one-sided limits agree; here the graph jumps, so no single value is approached.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the limit of (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) as x approaches 3.
quiz.explain: Factoring gives (x - 3)(x + 3)/(x - 3) = x + 3 for x not equal to 3, which approaches 6. The limit ignores what happens exactly at the point.

quiz.prompt: What does (2x^3 + x)/(x^2 + 1) do as x becomes very large?
quiz.answer: It grows beyond any bound
quiz.explain: The numerator has the higher degree, so the quotient behaves like 2x for large x and increases without limit. Ratios of leading coefficients apply when the degrees match.

quiz.prompt: A function equals x + 1 for x below 2 and equals x^2 for x above 2. Does the limit as x approaches 2 exist?
quiz.answer: No, the one-sided limits disagree
quiz.explain: From the left the values approach 3 and from the right they approach 4, so there is no single value the function nears. A limit exists only when both sides agree.

quiz.prompt: For which kind of function does substituting x = a straight into the formula give the correct limit as x approaches a?
quiz.answer: One that is continuous at a
choices: One that is continuous at a
One that has a hole at a
One that is undefined at a
quiz.explain: Continuity at a point means the limit and the function value agree there, which is exactly what makes substitution safe. Holes, jumps and gaps are the cases where you must work harder.

lesson_media.alt: A graph approaches height four from both sides while the function value at x equals two is shown at height two.
lesson_media.caption: A limit describes nearby values and can exist even when the function value is different or undefined.

nodes.title: Differential Calculus
nodes.goal: Derivatives: rates of change, optimization, curve sketching.

quiz.prompt: If f(x) = x^3, what is the value of f'(x) at x = 2?
The function f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 has a minimum. At what x-value does it occur?
quiz.explain: Setting f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 gives x = 2, the location of the minimum.

quiz.prompt: A ball's height is h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t meters. What is its velocity at t = 1 second?
quiz.answer: 10 m/s
quiz.explain: Velocity is h'(t) = -10t + 20, and at t = 1 that is 10 m/s.

quiz.prompt: A tank holds V(t) = 2t^3 + 5t litres after t seconds. Give the rate at which the volume is growing, in litres per second, at t = 3.
quiz.explain: V'(t) = 6t^2 + 5, and at t = 3 that is 54 + 5 = 59 litres per second.

quiz.prompt: A farmer has 40 m of fencing for a rectangular pen. Give the dimensions that enclose the greatest area.
quiz.answer: 10 m by 10 m
quiz.explain: With the perimeter fixed at 40 the two sides add to 20, so the area is x(20 - x), maximised at x = 10: the square beats every other rectangle. A 20 m by 20 m pen would need 80 m of fencing.

quiz.prompt: For a differentiable f, the derivative f' is positive on (0, 2), zero at 2, and positive again on (2, 5). Describe the behaviour of f at x = 2.
quiz.answer: A stationary point that is not a turning point
choices: A local maximum, since the derivative is zero there
A stretch on which f holds steady
A stationary point that is not a turning point
quiz.explain: The derivative touches zero without changing sign, so the curve flattens and then keeps rising, exactly as x^3 does at the origin. A zero derivative at one point neither holds f steady near it nor forces a turning point.

quiz.prompt: Suppose g(x) = x^2 e^x. Compute g'(1), then divide that value by e to get a whole number. Give that whole number.
quiz.explain: By the product rule g'(x) = 2x e^x + x^2 e^x, so g'(1) = 2e + e = 3e, which is 3 after dividing by e.

quiz.prompt: A student differentiates f(x) = sin(3x) and writes down cos(3x). Diagnose the mistake.
quiz.answer: The chain rule factor of 3 was dropped
choices: The chain rule factor of 3 was dropped
The minus sign belonging to sine was lost
The power rule was used instead of the chain rule
The inside factor should be 1/3 rather than 3
quiz.explain: Differentiating an inside function of 3x multiplies the result by 3, so the correct derivative is 3cos(3x). Dividing by 3 is what integrating sin(3x) would do.

quiz.prompt: Suppose a smooth function h satisfies h'(4) = 0 and h''(4) = -3. Predict the behaviour of h at that input.
quiz.answer: A local maximum
choices: A point where h is falling fastest
quiz.explain: A vanishing first derivative with a negative second derivative means the curve is concave down at a stationary point, which is a local maximum. Concave down is not the same as decreasing: h is momentarily flat there, not falling.

quiz.prompt: A student argues that because f(x) = |x| attains its smallest value at the origin, f'(0) must equal zero. Explain what is wrong with that reasoning.
quiz.answer: The absolute value graph has a corner at the origin, so f is not differentiable there and f'(0) does not exist at all; the rule that extrema occur where the derivative vanishes only applies at points where the derivative exists, and extrema can also sit at corners or endpoints.
quiz.explain: Interior extrema occur where the derivative is zero or undefined, and a sharp corner is the second case.

lesson_media.alt: A parabola shows secant lines through nearby points approaching a tangent, beside a corner with different one-sided slopes.
lesson_media.caption: A derivative is the limit of secant slopes when that limit exists. A minimum at a corner need not have derivative zero.

nodes.title: Integral Calculus
nodes.goal: Integrals: accumulation, area, the fundamental theorem.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the definite integral of 3x^2 from x = 0 to x = 2.
quiz.explain: An antiderivative is x^3, and evaluating gives 2^3 - 0^3 = 8.

quiz.prompt: What is the indefinite integral of 2x with respect to x?
quiz.answer: x^2 + C
quiz.explain: The antiderivative of 2x is x^2, plus a constant of integration C.

quiz.prompt: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, if F'(x) = f(x), then the definite integral of f from a to b equals which of the following?
quiz.answer: F(b) - F(a)
quiz.explain: The theorem evaluates the antiderivative at the endpoints: F(b) - F(a). Using f rather than its antiderivative F is the usual slip.

quiz.prompt: A car's velocity is v(t) = 6t metres per second between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds. Give the distance travelled, in metres.
quiz.explain: Distance is the integral of speed: the integral of 6t from 0 to 4 is 3t^2 at t = 4, which is 48 m.

quiz.prompt: Sketch the region caught between y = x and y = x^2 for x from 0 to 1, then give its area.
quiz.explain: The line lies above the parabola there, so the area is the integral of (x - x^2), which is 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.

quiz.prompt: The integral of f from 0 to 3 is 12, and the integral of f from 0 to 5 is 20. Give the integral of f from 3 to 5.
quiz.explain: Integrals add over adjacent intervals, so the piece from 3 to 5 is 20 - 12 = 8.

quiz.prompt: Water flows into a tank at a rate of r(t) = 4t + 1 litres per minute. Give the number of litres added between t = 0 and t = 3 minutes.
quiz.explain: Accumulated amount is the integral of the rate: 2t^2 + t evaluated at 3 gives 18 + 3 = 21 litres.

quiz.prompt: A student evaluates the integral of 1/x from -1 to 1 and reports a result of zero, citing symmetry. Diagnose the flaw.
quiz.answer: The ordinary improper integral diverges at zero
choices: The ordinary improper integral diverges at zero
1/x is even, so the two halves add rather than cancel
The limits of integration should have been swapped first
The antiderivative involved is a power rather than a logarithm
quiz.explain: The two one-sided improper integrals must converge separately, but both diverge at zero. A symmetric Cauchy principal value is 0, yet that is a different notion and does not make the ordinary improper integral converge.

quiz.prompt: Suppose G(x) accumulates the area under a positive, increasing function f starting from 0. Predict the shape of the graph of G.
quiz.answer: Rising, and bending upward
quiz.explain: G' = f is positive so G rises, and G'' = f' is positive so G is concave up.

quiz.prompt: A continuous function has average value 6 over the interval from 1 to 4. Give the value of its definite integral over that same interval.
quiz.explain: Average value is the integral divided by the interval width, so the integral is 6 times 3.

lesson_media.alt: A sign-changing curve has positive and negative shaded regions aligned with its accumulation function below.
lesson_media.caption: The definite integral accumulates signed change. The Fundamental Theorem links the accumulation function's slope to the original function.

nodes.title: Multivariable Calculus
nodes.goal: Partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus.

quiz.prompt: For f(x, y) = x^2 y + y^3, what is the partial derivative with respect to x?
quiz.answer: 2xy
quiz.explain: Treating y as a constant, the derivative of x^2 y is 2xy and the derivative of y^3 is 0.

quiz.prompt: For f(x, y) = x^2 y + y^3, what is the partial derivative with respect to y?
quiz.explain: Treating x as a constant, the derivative of x^2 y is x^2 and the derivative of y^3 is 3y^2.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the double integral of (x + y) over the unit square, with x from 0 to 1 and y from 0 to 1.
quiz.explain: The inner integral gives 1/2 + y, and integrating that from 0 to 1 gives 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.

quiz.prompt: For f(x, y) = x^2 y + y^3, give the value of the mixed partial derivative f_xy at the point (2, 1).
quiz.explain: f_x = 2xy, so f_xy = 2x, which is 4 at x = 2 whatever y may be.

quiz.prompt: At a point where the gradient of a smooth function of two variables vanishes, describe what the surface may be doing.
quiz.answer: A maximum, a minimum, or a saddle
choices: Only a maximum or a minimum
A flat patch of surface around the point
A maximum, a minimum, or a saddle
A minimum, since the gradient points uphill
quiz.explain: A vanishing gradient marks a critical point; the second-derivative test then decides between the peak, the pit and the saddle. A zero gradient at one point says nothing about the surface nearby, so it need not be flat there.

quiz.prompt: A hiker stands on a hillside where the gradient of the height function points due north. To lose height as fast as possible, name the direction to walk.
quiz.answer: Due south
quiz.explain: The gradient points the way of steepest ascent, so the steepest descent lies exactly opposite it.

quiz.prompt: At a critical point of a smooth function, a student computes f_xx = 2, f_yy = 8, and f_xy = 6. Decide what the second derivative test reports.
quiz.answer: A saddle point
choices: A case the test leaves undecided
quiz.explain: The discriminant f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2 = 16 - 36 = -20 is negative, which signals a saddle.

quiz.prompt: For f(x, y) = x^2 + 3xy + y^2, compute the directional derivative at the point (1, 1) in the direction of the unit vector pointing along (3, 4).
quiz.explain: The gradient there is (5, 5), and dotting with the unit vector (0.6, 0.8) gives 3 + 4 = 7.

quiz.prompt: A vector field models fluid velocity, and throughout a small ball its divergence is negative. What does that sign establish directly?
quiz.answer: The net local flux is inward: the velocity field contracts volume there
choices: The net local flux is inward: the velocity field contracts volume there
Fluid is speeding up as it passes through
quiz.explain: Divergence measures net outflow per unit volume, so a negative value gives local volume contraction or net inward flux. Whether density increases also depends on the continuity equation and the density field; rotation is measured separately by curl.

quiz.prompt: Suppose you swap the order of integration in a double integral over a triangular region. Explain what has to be rewritten and what stays fixed.
quiz.answer: The inner and outer limits must be recomputed by re-describing the same triangle with the other variable on the outside, while the region itself and the numerical value of the integral are unchanged; Fubini's theorem guarantees the two orders agree for a well-behaved integrand.
quiz.explain: Swapping order changes only the bookkeeping of the limits, not the region or the answer.

lesson_media.alt: A saddle's contour map marks a point, its two coordinate slices, the gradient and a chosen direction.
lesson_media.caption: Partial derivatives are coordinate-slice slopes. The gradient packages them, and its dot product with a unit vector gives directional change.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.goal: Vector spaces, matrices, eigenvalues — the language of modern science.

lesson_media.alt: The same marked unit square remains a square under identity, shears into an equal-area parallelogram, and projects to a line as distinct vertices merge.
lesson_media.caption: Determinant tracks signed area scaling: identity and shear have determinant one, while projection has determinant zero, collapses area, and cannot be inverted.

lesson_media.title: Transform the plane
lesson_media.instructions: Choose a fixed 2-by-2 matrix. Compare the original grid, basis vectors and vector v with their images, then use the determinant to predict area scaling and invertibility.

quiz.prompt: Compute the determinant of the matrix [[2, 1], [3, 4]].
What are the eigenvalues of the diagonal matrix [[3, 0], [0, 5]]?
quiz.answer: 3 and 5
quiz.explain: The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are exactly its diagonal entries, 3 and 5. The vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) are its eigenvectors, which answers a different question: an eigenvalue is the number a vector is stretched by, not the vector itself. The 8 and 15 are the trace and the determinant.

quiz.prompt: For which values of k does the system kx + 2y = 1 and 8x + ky = 4 fail to have a unique solution?
quiz.answer: k = 4 or k = -4
quiz.explain: A square system has a unique solution exactly when the determinant is nonzero. Here the determinant is k^2 - 16, which vanishes at k = 4 and at k = -4; at those two values the lines are parallel and there is no solution at all.
choices: Every value of k gives a unique solution

quiz.prompt: A 3x3 matrix has eigenvalues 2, 3 and 5. Give its determinant.
quiz.explain: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity: 2 x 3 x 5 = 30.

quiz.prompt: Three vectors in R^3 turn out to span only a plane. Give the rank of the 3x3 matrix whose columns they are.
quiz.explain: Rank is the dimension of the column space, and a plane through the origin has dimension 2, so the matrix is singular.

quiz.prompt: A matrix A satisfies Av = 4v for some nonzero vector v. Work out what A^3 does to that same v.
quiz.answer: It sends v to 64v
choices: It sends v to 12v, tripling the eigenvalue
It cannot be told without knowing the entries of A
It sends v to 4v, since eigenvalues persist
quiz.explain: Applying A three times multiplies v by 4 each time, so A^3 v = 4^3 v = 64v. The eigenvalue of A^3 is the cube of the eigenvalue of A, and nothing else about A is needed.

quiz.prompt: A 4-by-4 matrix turns out to have rank three. Give the dimension of its null space.
quiz.explain: The rank-nullity theorem gives rank plus nullity equal to the number of columns, so the nullity is 4 - 3.

quiz.prompt: A student insists that a 3-by-3 matrix with two identical columns is still invertible, because none of its entries vanish. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: Repeated columns are dependent, so the determinant is zero
choices: Repeated columns are dependent, so the determinant is zero
The determinant is nonzero as long as no row is all zeros
Repeated columns force the matrix to be symmetric
Repeated columns lower the rank but leave the determinant alone
quiz.explain: Invertibility depends on independent columns, not on whether entries happen to be nonzero. Two equal columns make the determinant vanish, and a vanishing determinant is exactly a drop in rank: the two go together.

quiz.prompt: Suppose a 2-by-2 matrix A has eigenvalues 0.5 and 0.9. Predict what repeatedly applying A does to a typical starting vector.
quiz.answer: It shrinks toward the origin
choices: It settles onto the eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.9
It settles onto a nonzero fixed vector
quiz.explain: Both eigenvalues have magnitude below one, so every component decays and the vector collapses to the origin. Its direction does line up with the 0.9-eigenvector, but the length still goes to zero, so nothing nonzero survives.

quiz.prompt: A linear map on R^3 has trace 7, and two of its three eigenvalues are 1 and 2. Give the remaining eigenvalue.
quiz.explain: The trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues, so the third is 7 - 1 - 2.

nodes.title: Differential Equations
nodes.goal: Model change: first and second order ODEs.

quiz.prompt: What is the general solution of the differential equation dy/dx = y?
quiz.answer: y = Ce^x
quiz.explain: A function equal to its own derivative is the exponential, y = Ce^x.

quiz.prompt: A drug leaves the bloodstream at a rate proportional to the amount still present, and a 100 mg dose falls to 50 mg in 4 hours. Give the amount left after 12 hours.
quiz.explain: dA/dt = -kA gives exponential decay with a fixed half-life, here 4 hours. Twelve hours is three half-lives, so 100 mg falls to 50, then 25, then 12.5 mg. The decay removes a fixed fraction each period, not a fixed amount.
choices: Nothing, since it loses 50 mg every 4 hours

quiz.prompt: Given dy/dx = 3 with y(0) = 2, find y(4).
quiz.explain: Integrating gives y = 3x + 2, so y(4) = 12 + 2 = 14.

quiz.prompt: A population obeys dP/dt = 0.2P with P(0) = 50. Give P at t = 10, rounded to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The solution is P = 50 e^(0.2t), so P(10) = 50 e^2, which is about 369.45.

quiz.prompt: A cup of coffee at 90 C is left in a 20 C room and cools by Newton's law. Describe its temperature in the long run.
quiz.answer: It decays toward 20 C, approaching but not reaching it
choices: It falls to 20 C and then keeps falling
It falls in a straight line until it hits 20 C
It settles at the average of 90 and 20
It decays toward 20 C, approaching but not reaching it
quiz.explain: The gap between coffee and room shrinks exponentially, so the temperature closes on 20 C without quite arriving.

quiz.prompt: A mass on a spring obeys y'' + 9y = 0. Give the general form of the solutions.
quiz.answer: A cos(3t) + B sin(3t)
quiz.explain: The characteristic roots are +3i and -3i, so the motion oscillates at angular frequency 3 rather than 9.

quiz.prompt: A sample decays according to dN/dt = -kN and loses half its mass every 5 days. Give the number of days it takes to fall to one eighth of the starting mass.
quiz.explain: One eighth is three successive halvings, and each halving takes 5 days.

quiz.prompt: A student solves y'' + 4y' + 4y = 0 and writes y = Ae^(-2t) + Be^(-2t). Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: The repeated root needs a second solution of the form t e^(-2t)
choices: The repeated root needs a second solution of the form t e^(-2t)
The characteristic roots should have been complex conjugates
The signs in the exponents were reversed during solving
A second order equation carries just one arbitrary constant
quiz.explain: The characteristic equation has the double root -2, so the second independent solution picks up a factor of t.

quiz.prompt: Suppose a logistic model dP/dt = 0.4P(1 - P/500) starts from P(0) = 600. Predict the long-run behaviour of P.
quiz.answer: It declines toward 500
quiz.explain: Above the carrying capacity the growth rate is negative, so the population falls back toward 500.

quiz.prompt: Explain how a direction field lets someone sketch solution curves of dy/dx = f(x, y) without ever finding a formula for y.
quiz.answer: At each point of the plane the equation hands you the slope of any solution passing through it, so drawing short tangent segments on a grid shows the local direction everywhere; a solution curve is then traced by following those segments, which reveals the qualitative behaviour even when no closed-form solution exists.
quiz.explain: The equation is itself a slope recipe, so the geometry of solutions is available before any integration.

lesson_media.alt: A logistic slope field shows solutions rising toward, staying on, or falling toward a carrying-capacity line.
lesson_media.caption: A differential equation assigns a local slope. An initial condition selects one solution, and equilibria organize its long-run behavior.

nodes.title: Discrete Mathematics
nodes.goal: Logic, sets, graphs, and counting.

quiz.prompt: How many ways can you choose 2 items from a set of 5, when order does not matter?
In a complete graph on 5 vertices, every vertex connects to every other. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: Each edge joins a distinct pair of vertices, so there are C(5,2) = 10 edges.

quiz.prompt: How many different 3-letter arrangements can be made using distinct letters chosen from {A, B, C, D}?
quiz.explain: Order matters, so this is P(4,3) = 4 x 3 x 2 = 24.

quiz.prompt: Eight people sit around a circular table, and two seatings count as the same when one is a rotation of the other. Give the number of distinct seatings.
quiz.explain: Fixing one person to kill the rotations leaves 7! = 5040 arrangements of the rest.

quiz.prompt: A simple graph has six vertices, each of degree 3. Give the number of edges.
quiz.explain: The degrees sum to 18, and each edge is counted twice in that sum, so there are 9 edges.

quiz.prompt: You drop 13 letters into 12 pigeonholes. State what must be true.
quiz.answer: Some hole holds at least two letters
choices: Each hole holds at least one letter
Exactly one hole receives more than one letter
Some hole holds at least two letters
One hole holds exactly two letters
quiz.explain: The pigeonhole principle guarantees a hole with two or more, but says nothing about which hole, how many such holes there are, or whether every hole is used at all.

quiz.prompt: In a round-robin tournament each of nine teams plays every other team exactly once. Give the total number of games played.
quiz.explain: Each game is a pair of teams, and the number of pairs from nine teams is 9 x 8 / 2.

quiz.prompt: A student claims that a connected graph on ten vertices with nine edges has to contain a cycle. Diagnose the claim.
quiz.answer: It is a tree, and trees contain no cycles
choices: It is a tree, and trees contain no cycles
Nine edges are too few to connect ten vertices at all
Connectedness on its own already forces a cycle
Any graph with more vertices than edges contains a cycle
quiz.explain: A connected graph on n vertices with exactly n - 1 edges is a tree, and trees contain no cycles. Nine edges are precisely enough to connect ten vertices, and having fewer edges than vertices makes a cycle less likely, not more.

quiz.prompt: A password uses four characters drawn from a 26-letter alphabet, and repeats are permitted. A student counts the possibilities as 26 x 25 x 24 x 23. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: Each of the four slots keeps all 26 options, so 26^4
choices: Each of the four slots keeps all 26 options, so 26^4
Order is irrelevant, so a binomial coefficient is needed
The alphabet size should shrink by one at each step
The base and exponent are swapped: it should be 4^26
quiz.explain: Permitting repetition means each of the four slots independently has 26 options, giving 26^4 = 456,976. The falling product 26 x 25 x 24 x 23 counts only the passwords whose four characters are all different.

quiz.prompt: Explain how the pigeonhole principle settles the question of whether two people in a group of thirteen must share a birth month.
quiz.answer: There are twelve months but thirteen people, so treating the months as pigeonholes and the people as pigeons means at least one month receives two or more people; whenever the number of items exceeds the number of categories, some category has to hold more than one item.
quiz.explain: The principle needs only a count comparison, not any knowledge of birthday patterns.

lesson_media.alt: Five labeled vertices are joined by all ten possible edges, with a tally matching edges to unordered pairs.
lesson_media.caption: In a simple complete graph, each edge is one unordered pair. Summing degrees counts every edge twice.

nodes.title: Number Theory
nodes.goal: Primes, congruences, and why they guard your secrets.

quiz.prompt: What is 17 mod 5?
quiz.explain: 17 = 3 x 5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

quiz.prompt: What is the greatest common divisor of 48 and 36?
quiz.explain: 48 = 12 x 4 and 36 = 12 x 3, and 12 is the largest number dividing both.

quiz.prompt: Compute (7 x 8) mod 5.
quiz.explain: 7 x 8 = 56, and 56 = 11 x 5 + 1, so the result is 1.

quiz.prompt: Give the remainder when 2^100 is divided by 7.
quiz.explain: Powers of 2 cycle mod 7 as 2, 4, 1 with period 3, and 100 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, so 2^100 is congruent to 2.

quiz.prompt: Solve the congruence 3x congruent to 1 modulo 7, taking x from 0 to 6.
quiz.explain: 3 x 5 = 15 = 2 x 7 + 1, so 5 is the multiplicative inverse of 3 modulo 7.

quiz.prompt: RSA rests on a gap: multiplying two large primes is easy, while factoring their product is hard. Suppose someone publishes a fast factoring algorithm. Work out which part of the scheme collapses.
quiz.answer: The private key, which is recoverable from the public modulus
choices: Key generation, which relies on producing two large primes quickly
The private key, which is recoverable from the public modulus
Encryption, which could no longer scramble the message
Nothing, since the modulus was public from the start
quiz.explain: Factoring the public modulus n recovers the secret primes p and q, hence (p - 1)(q - 1) and the private exponent. Generating keys and encrypting messages would still work exactly as before; what is lost is the secrecy of the private key, which is the whole of the security.

quiz.prompt: Give the final digit of 7 raised to the power 2023.
quiz.explain: Last digits of powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1, and 2023 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4, landing on 3.

quiz.prompt: Knowing that a prime dividing a product must divide one of the factors, a student concludes that if 6 divides ab then 6 divides a or 6 divides b. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: Six is composite, so Euclid's lemma does not apply
choices: Six is composite, so Euclid's lemma does not apply
The lemma requires ab itself to be a prime number
Euclid's lemma extends to composite divisors as well
Euclid's lemma applies only when a and b are themselves prime
quiz.explain: Euclid's lemma holds for prime divisors; 6 divides 2 x 3 without dividing either factor. The factors a and b need not be prime for the lemma to be used, only the divisor must be.

quiz.prompt: Give how many positive integers less than 20 share no common factor above 1 with 20.
quiz.explain: Euler's totient of 20 is 20 x (1/2) x (4/5) = 8, counting 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17 and 19.

quiz.prompt: Suppose Fermat's little theorem is applied to work out 5^12 modulo 13. Predict the outcome together with the reason.
quiz.answer: One, since 12 is 13 minus one
choices: Zero, since the modulus divides that power
Five, since the base carries through unchanged
It cannot be found without computing 5^12 in full
quiz.explain: Fermat's little theorem says a^(p-1) is congruent to 1 mod p whenever p does not divide a. Here p = 13 and the exponent is 12, so the value is 1 with no computation; a^p congruent to a is the variant that would leave 5.

lesson_media.alt: A seven-position residue clock traces powers of two through the repeating cycle one, two, four, one.
lesson_media.caption: Congruence keeps only the remainder class. Repeated powers enter cycles, which make huge exponents manageable.

nodes.title: Real Analysis
nodes.goal: Calculus made rigorous: epsilon, delta, convergence.

quiz.prompt: To what value does the sequence a_n = 1/n converge as n grows large?
quiz.explain: As n increases without bound, 1/n becomes arbitrarily small, converging to 0. There is no smallest positive real number for it to stop at: whatever candidate you name, some 1/n is smaller still.
choices: A positive number smaller than every other

quiz.prompt: A reader is proving that 3x tends to 6 as x tends to 2 straight from the epsilon-delta definition, and is handed epsilon = 0.06. Pick the delta that does the job, with the reason.
quiz.answer: 0.02, because 3 times 0.02 is 0.06
quiz.explain: The requirement is |3x - 6| < 0.06 whenever |x - 2| < delta. Since |3x - 6| is 3|x - 2|, taking delta = 0.06 / 3 = 0.02 works. Matching delta to epsilon would let |3x - 6| reach 0.18.
choices: Any delta works once epsilon is fixed

quiz.prompt: Which of these sequences does NOT converge?
quiz.explain: (-1)^n alternates between -1 and 1 forever and never settles on a single limit.

quiz.prompt: The sequence a_n = (-1)^n stays inside [-1, 1] but has no limit. Say what Bolzano-Weierstrass still guarantees here, and what the even-numbered and odd-numbered terms do.
quiz.answer: Because the sequence is bounded it must have a convergent subsequence: the even-numbered terms converge to 1 and the odd-numbered terms converge to -1, so boundedness delivers subsequential limits without delivering convergence.
quiz.explain: Bolzano-Weierstrass promises a convergent subsequence for any bounded sequence; two different subsequential limits are exactly why the whole sequence cannot converge.

quiz.prompt: Let f(x) = x^2 sin(1/x) for x nonzero, with f(0) = 0. Decide what happens at the origin.
quiz.answer: f is differentiable at 0, with f'(0) = 0
choices: f has an infinite derivative at 0
f is differentiable at 0, with f'(0) = 0
f is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there
quiz.explain: The difference quotient is x sin(1/x). The squeeze theorem says: if a function is trapped between two others that both converge to the same limit, it converges there too — and since sin(1/x) always stays between -1 and 1, x sin(1/x) is trapped between -|x| and |x|, both of which go to 0 as x goes to 0. So the difference quotient goes to 0, and the derivative exists, even though f' itself is not continuous at 0.

quiz.prompt: A sequence of continuous functions on [0, 1] converges pointwise to a limit that has a jump. Decide which conclusion is safe.
quiz.answer: The convergence cannot be uniform
choices: Some f_n must itself be discontinuous
Pointwise limits of continuous maps stay continuous
The limit is continuous except at finitely many points
quiz.explain: A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so a jump rules uniform convergence out; pointwise convergence carries no such promise.

quiz.prompt: A student argues that the series with terms 1/n converges, since those terms shrink toward zero. Diagnose the reasoning.
quiz.answer: Shrinking terms are necessary but not sufficient
choices: Shrinking terms are necessary but not sufficient
The harmonic series does converge to a finite value
The terms should be compared against 1/n^2 instead
The terms shrink too slowly for the test to say anything
quiz.explain: The harmonic series diverges even though its terms tend to zero, so the vanishing-terms test can only rule convergence out, never establish it.

quiz.prompt: Suppose f is continuous on [0, 1] with f(0) = -2 and f(1) = 3. Predict what has to occur somewhere inside the interval.
quiz.answer: Some point at which f takes the value zero exactly
choices: Some point at which f takes the value zero exactly
A stretch on which f is increasing
Every value from -2 to 3, each reached just once
A greatest value of 3, reached inside the interval
quiz.explain: The intermediate value theorem forces a continuous function to take every value between -2 and 3, so zero is reached at least once. It promises nothing about uniqueness, about f increasing anywhere, or about where the largest value sits.

quiz.prompt: A sequence of rational numbers is Cauchy yet has no rational limit. Explain what this reveals about the rationals and how the reals repair it.
quiz.answer: It shows the rationals are not complete: a sequence whose terms crowd arbitrarily close together can still fail to have a limit inside the rationals, as with decimal approximations to the square root of 2. The reals are constructed precisely so that every Cauchy sequence converges, which is the completeness axiom.
quiz.explain: Completeness is the property that distinguishes the real line from the rational line and underwrites limits in analysis.

quiz.prompt: Consider the set of numbers of the form 1 - 1/n as n ranges over the positive integers. Give its least upper bound.
quiz.explain: The values climb toward 1 without reaching it, so 1 is the supremum even though it is not a member of the set.

lesson_media.alt: Epsilon and delta bands around a line show every nearby input mapping into a required output band.
lesson_media.caption: The limit definition controls every punctured-neighborhood input, not just sampled points. Delta may depend on epsilon.

nodes.title: Probability Theory
nodes.goal: Random variables, distributions, the law of large numbers.

quiz.prompt: What is the expected value of a single roll of a fair six-sided die?
quiz.explain: The average of 1 through 6 is (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5.

quiz.prompt: A fair die is rolled 6,000 times. Predict what the law of large numbers actually promises about the proportion of sixes and about the count of sixes.
quiz.answer: The proportion nears 1/6 though the count may miss by tens
quiz.explain: The law of large numbers is a statement about the sample proportion, which converges to 1/6. The count of sixes has standard deviation sqrt(6000 x (1/6) x (5/6)), about 29, so it typically sits tens away from 1,000 and that gap does not shrink.
choices: Both the proportion and the count close in on their targets
The proportion nears 1/6 though the count may miss by tens
Neither settles, since every roll is random

quiz.prompt: A random variable X is uniform on the integers 1 through 10. What is P(X > 7)?
quiz.explain: The favorable outcomes are 8, 9, and 10, giving 3 of 10 equally likely values.

quiz.prompt: X counts the successes in 20 independent trials, each succeeding with probability 0.3. Give the variance of X.
quiz.explain: For a binomial variable the variance is np(1 - p) = 20 x 0.3 x 0.7 = 4.2.

quiz.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and X is their total. Compare the chance that X = 7 with the chance that X = 2.
quiz.answer: X = 7 is six times as likely
choices: X = 7 is six times as likely
quiz.explain: Six of the 36 outcomes total 7 but only one totals 2, so the ratio is 6 to 1.

quiz.prompt: A casino game has an expected value of -5 cents per play. Predict a regular player's average result per play after many thousands of plays.
quiz.answer: A loss of about 5 cents per play
choices: A loss that shrinks with practice
A loss of about 5 cents in total over all the plays
A loss of about 5 cents per play
quiz.explain: The law of large numbers pulls the sample mean toward the expected value, so the average loss per play settles near 5 cents. Over thousands of plays that compounds into a large total, and practice cannot move a fixed expected value.

quiz.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Give the standard deviation of the number of heads obtained.
quiz.explain: For a binomial count the variance is npq = 100 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 25, whose square root is 5.

quiz.prompt: After seeing ten heads in a row from a fair coin, a student predicts that tails has become more likely. Diagnose the reasoning.
quiz.answer: Independent flips carry no memory of the past
choices: Independent flips carry no memory of the past
The law of large numbers forces a swift correction
A run that long proves the coin favours tails
Earlier outcomes lower the chance of another head
quiz.explain: This is the gambler's fallacy: independence means each flip stays at one half regardless of history.

quiz.prompt: A condition affects 1 person in 1,000. A screening test flags 99 percent of those who have it and 1 percent of those who do not. Out of 100,000 people screened, work out how many of the flagged actually have the condition and how many do not.
quiz.answer: About 99 do and about 999 do not
choices: About 99 do and about 999 do not
About 99 do and about 1 does not, since the test is 99 percent right
About 990 do and about 999 do not
About 999 have it and about 99 do not
quiz.explain: Of 100,000 people about 100 have the condition, and 99 of those are flagged. Of the 99,900 who do not, 1 percent — about 999 — are flagged anyway. So roughly 1,098 flags contain only 99 true cases, fewer than one in ten.

quiz.prompt: A random variable X has mean 10 and variance 4, and Y is defined by Y = 3X + 2. Give the variance of Y.
quiz.explain: Adding a constant leaves spread alone while a scale factor of 3 multiplies the variance by 9, giving 9 x 4.

lesson_media.alt: Three checkpoints compare a coin's running heads proportion with one half while the raw count difference still fluctuates.
lesson_media.caption: The law of large numbers concerns long-run proportions under stated assumptions. It does not force short runs to balance or counts to stay close.

nodes.title: Complex Numbers and Beyond
nodes.goal: The plane where every nonconstant polynomial has a root.

quiz.prompt: Compute (2 + 3i) + (1 - i).
quiz.explain: Add real parts and imaginary parts separately: (2 + 1) + (3 - 1)i = 3 + 2i.

quiz.prompt: What is the value of i^2?
quiz.explain: The imaginary unit is defined so that i^2 = -1.

quiz.prompt: What is the modulus (absolute value) of the complex number 3 + 4i?
quiz.explain: The modulus is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.

quiz.prompt: Write (1 + i)^8 in the form a + bi and give the real part a.
quiz.explain: (1 + i)^2 = 2i, so (1 + i)^4 = -4 and (1 + i)^8 = 16, a real number.

quiz.prompt: Multiply 2(cos 30 + i sin 30) by 3(cos 60 + i sin 60), and give the product in the form a + bi.
quiz.answer: 6i
quiz.explain: Multiplying in polar form multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments: modulus 6 at 90 degrees, which is 6i.

quiz.prompt: Use de Moivre's theorem to work out how many distinct complex cube roots 8 has, and where they sit in the plane.
quiz.answer: Three, equally spaced on a circle of radius 2
choices: Three, lying along the real axis
Three, equally spaced on a circle of radius 2
quiz.explain: De Moivre's theorem says (r(cos θ + i sin θ))^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ) — raising a complex number in polar form to a power multiplies its angle by that power. Taking an nth root runs this in reverse: divide the angle by n (and take the nth root of the modulus) to get one root, then add 360/n degrees repeatedly to get the rest. Each nonzero complex number has exactly n distinct nth roots this way; here 8 = 8(cos 0 + i sin 0) gives cube roots at modulus 2, angles 0, 120, and 240 degrees — evenly spaced round a circle of radius 2.

quiz.prompt: Give the smallest positive integer n for which (1 + i)^n comes out as a positive real number.
quiz.explain: The number 1 + i has argument 45 degrees, so the argument reaches a full 360 degrees at n = 8, where the value is 16.

quiz.prompt: A student declares that z^2 = -9 has no solutions, since squares cannot be negative. Diagnose the claim.
quiz.answer: Two of them: 3i and -3i
choices: None, because a square is never negative
quiz.explain: Squares of real numbers are nonnegative, but i^2 = -1, so (3i)^2 = -9 and (-3i)^2 = -9 as well. Both roots count, and (9i)^2 is -81 rather than -9.

quiz.prompt: Suppose a polynomial with real coefficients has 2 - 5i among its roots. Predict a further root it must have.
quiz.answer: The conjugate, 2 + 5i
quiz.explain: Real coefficients force non-real roots to arrive in conjugate pairs, so 2 + 5i must also be a root. Flipping the sign of the real part is not conjugation, and the pairing is compulsory rather than optional.

quiz.prompt: Explain, in terms of rotation and scaling, what multiplying a complex number by i does to its position in the plane.
quiz.answer: Multiplying by i rotates the point 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin and leaves its distance from the origin unchanged, because i has modulus 1 and argument 90 degrees, and multiplication adds arguments while multiplying moduli.
quiz.explain: Complex multiplication multiplies lengths and adds angles, so a factor of i is a pure quarter turn.

lesson_media.alt: Multiplying one plus i by i rotates its point ninety degrees counterclockwise without changing its distance from the origin.
lesson_media.caption: Complex multiplication multiplies moduli and adds their directed arguments.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
nodes.goal: Groups, rings, fields — structure itself as an object of study.

quiz.prompt: A group must have closure, associativity, an identity, and inverses. Which of these is NOT a group?
quiz.answer: The positive integers under addition
quiz.explain: The natural numbers have no additive identity (0 is excluded) and no inverses, so they fail the group axioms.
choices: The integers modulo 5 under clock addition
The rational numbers under ordinary addition

quiz.prompt: In the integers mod 6 under addition, what is the additive inverse of 4?
quiz.explain: 4 + 2 = 6, which is congruent to 0 mod 6, so 2 is the inverse of 4. An inverse is what returns you to the identity, not the identity itself, and -4 has to be reduced mod 6 before it names an element.
choices: 0, which is the identity rather than the inverse
4, since 4 is its own inverse here

quiz.prompt: The integers mod 6, with addition and multiplication mod 6, form a ring but not a field. Diagnose which requirement they fail.
quiz.answer: Every nonzero element must be invertible
quiz.explain: The integers mod 6 do have a 1, their multiplication is commutative, and finite fields certainly exist — the integers mod 5 are one. What fails is invertibility: 2, 3 and 4 each share a factor with 6, so none of them has a reciprocal.
choices: Every nonzero element must be invertible
There must be a multiplicative identity

quiz.prompt: Let G be a group of order 15. Work out what Sylow's theorems force about the number of subgroups of order 5 and of order 3, and hence identify G.
quiz.answer: The number of Sylow 5-subgroups divides 3 and leaves remainder 1 on division by 5, so it is 1; the same counting makes the subgroup of order 3 unique. Both are therefore normal, they meet only in the identity, and G is their direct product, which is cyclic of order 15.
quiz.explain: Sylow's theorems say that for a prime p dividing |G|, a subgroup of the largest possible p-power order always exists, and the number of such subgroups divides the remaining (non-p) part of |G| while also leaving remainder 1 when divided by p. Applied here: the count of order-5 subgroups must divide 3 and be 1 more than a multiple of 5, so it is 1; the same counting makes the order-3 subgroup unique too. A unique subgroup of a given order is automatically normal, and a product of normal subgroups of coprime order is cyclic, so every group of order 15 is Z/15.

quiz.prompt: The cyclic group of order 4 and the Klein four-group both have four elements. Separate them with a single structural fact.
quiz.answer: Only one has an element of order 4
choices: Only one of them contains an element of order 2
Only one has an element of order 4
quiz.explain: The cyclic group is built from a generator of order 4, while in the Klein group every non-identity element squares to the identity. Both groups are abelian and both contain elements of order 2, so neither of those tests separates them.

quiz.prompt: H is a subgroup of a group G with 20 elements. Pick the order that H cannot have.
quiz.explain: Lagrange's theorem forces the order of a subgroup to divide the order of the group, and 8 does not divide 20.

quiz.prompt: A student defines f(n) = 3n from the integers under addition to themselves and calls it an isomorphism of that group onto itself. Diagnose the flaw.
quiz.answer: It is injective but its image is just the multiples of three
choices: It is injective but its image is just the multiples of three
It fails to preserve the addition operation
It sends the identity to a nonzero element
It has no inverse defined on its image
quiz.explain: f is a homomorphism and one-to-one, but it misses 1, so it is not surjective. An injective endomorphism of an infinite group need not be an automorphism.

quiz.prompt: In the symmetric group on four letters, count the elements of order four.
quiz.explain: Elements of order four are exactly the 4-cycles, and there are 3! = 6 of them. The 3-cycles, by contrast, have order three.

quiz.prompt: Working in the integers mod twelve, a student argues that 3x = 0 forces x to vanish, as it would over the rationals. Predict the actual solution set.
quiz.answer: Three elements: 0, 4 and 8
choices: Only the element 0, as over the rationals
quiz.explain: Twelve is not prime, so the ring has zero divisors: 3 x 4 = 12 and 3 x 8 = 24 both vanish mod 12, alongside 3 x 0. Cancellation belongs to integral domains, not to every ring. The multiples of 3 are what 3x runs through, not what solves 3x = 0.

quiz.prompt: A ring homomorphism sends a field F into a nonzero ring R and carries 1 to 1. Argue from ideals that the map must be injective.
quiz.answer: The kernel is an ideal of F, and a field has only the zero ideal and F itself as ideals. The kernel cannot be all of F, because 1 maps to the nonzero identity of R. So the kernel is the zero ideal, which makes the map injective.
quiz.explain: Fields have no proper nonzero ideals, so any unital homomorphism out of a field is either injective or sends everything to zero. This is why field extensions are always embeddings.

lesson_media.alt: Two four-element operation tables reveal different element orders in the cyclic and Klein four-groups.
lesson_media.caption: Groups can have the same number of elements yet different structure. Element orders distinguish the cyclic group C4 from the Klein four-group.

nodes.title: Measure Theory
nodes.goal: Lebesgue integration and the foundations of probability.

quiz.prompt: Cover the n-th rational in the unit interval by an open interval of length epsilon/2^n. Use that cover to decide the Lebesgue measure of the rationals there.
quiz.explain: The covering intervals have total length at most epsilon, and epsilon may be taken as small as you like, so the measure is squeezed to zero.

quiz.prompt: Lebesgue's construction slices by output value: for each value the function takes, it measures the set of inputs where that value occurs. Apply this to a function on [0, 1] that equals 8 on a set of measure 1/4 and 0 elsewhere, and give the integral.
quiz.answer: 2, that is 8 times 1/4
quiz.explain: Slicing by output gives two bands: the value 8 on a set of measure 1/4 contributes 8 x 1/4 = 2, and the value 0 contributes nothing. The construction never asks the function to be continuous, so jumps are no obstacle.
choices: 8, the value taken on the set
It is undefined, since the function jumps

quiz.prompt: Two functions on [0, 1] agree everywhere except at the points 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and so on. Decide whether they are equal almost everywhere, and what that means for their integrals.
quiz.answer: Yes, and the two integrals match
quiz.explain: The exceptional set is countable and therefore has measure zero, so the two functions agree almost everywhere however many points are involved. The Lebesgue integral ignores sets of measure zero, so the integrals must match.
choices: Yes, and the two integrals match
No, since they differ at infinitely many points
Yes, but the integrals can still differ
Only if both functions are continuous

quiz.prompt: Define f on [0, 1] by f = 1 at each irrational point and f = 0 at each rational point. Give the Lebesgue integral of f over [0, 1].
quiz.explain: The rationals have measure zero, so f equals 1 almost everywhere and the integral is 1, even though the Riemann integral does not exist.

quiz.prompt: Let f_n equal n on the interval (0, 1/n) and 0 elsewhere on [0, 1]. Each f_n integrates to 1, yet f_n tends to 0 pointwise. Name the hypothesis of the dominated convergence theorem that fails.
quiz.answer: No single integrable function dominates every f_n
choices: No single integrable function dominates every f_n
quiz.explain: A dominating g would have to exceed n on (0, 1/n) for each n, forcing g above 1/x near the origin, and 1/x is not integrable there.

quiz.prompt: A bounded subset of the line has outer measure 1/2 and inner measure 1/3. Decide what follows.
quiz.answer: It fails to be Lebesgue measurable
choices: It fails to be Lebesgue measurable
It is measurable, with measure somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2
It is measurable, and its measure is the outer one, 1/2
quiz.explain: Lebesgue measurability asks the inner and outer measures to agree; a gap between them is the signature of a non-measurable set, and no value in between gets assigned to it.

quiz.prompt: Build a Cantor-style set in the unit interval by deleting open middle pieces whose lengths total one half. Predict the resulting set's measure and interior.
quiz.answer: Measure 1/2, and it contains no interval
choices: Measure 1/2, and it contains no interval
Measure zero, like the usual Cantor set
Measure 1/2, and it contains an interval
Measure zero, though it is uncountable
quiz.explain: This fat Cantor set is nowhere dense yet has measure one half, showing that being topologically small and being measure-theoretically small are independent notions.

quiz.prompt: Let mu be Lebesgue measure on the unit interval plus twice a point mass at x = 1/2. Compute the integral of f(x) = x with respect to mu over that interval.
quiz.explain: The Lebesgue part contributes 1/2 and the atom contributes 2 times f(1/2) = 1, for a total of 1.5. Integrals against a sum of measures add termwise.

quiz.prompt: Functions h_n tend pointwise to h on the unit interval, with each |h_n| at most 5. A student says dominated convergence fails here because constants are not integrable. Diagnose.
quiz.answer: On a set of finite measure the constant function is integrable, so the theorem does apply
choices: On a set of finite measure the constant function is integrable, so the theorem does apply
The student is right, and Fatou's lemma must be used instead
The theorem needs uniform convergence, which was not assumed
Integrability of the limit h has to be assumed separately
quiz.explain: A constant c is integrable over a finite-measure set, with integral c times the measure. Constants fail to be integrable only over sets of infinite measure, such as the whole line.

quiz.prompt: A student proposes assigning a length to every subset of the line so that the assignment is translation invariant and countably additive. Explain how the Vitali construction blocks this.
quiz.answer: Partition the unit interval by the relation x minus y rational and use choice to pick one representative per class. The rational translates of that set by rationals in a bounded range are disjoint and cover a bounded interval. Translation invariance gives all translates the same measure, so countable additivity yields a total that is either zero or infinite, never a finite positive length. So the set cannot be measurable.
quiz.explain: The clash between translation invariance and countable additivity is why Lebesgue measure is defined on a sigma-algebra rather than on the full power set.

lesson_media.alt: Shrinking open intervals cover an enumerated finite prefix of rational points while their total length stays below a chosen budget.
lesson_media.caption: A countable set can be dense yet have measure zero because covers can have arbitrarily small total length. The drawing shows only a finite prefix.

nodes.title: Topology
nodes.goal: Continuity without distance; the shape of space.

quiz.prompt: Stretching and bending may not change the number of holes running through an object. A sculptor starts with a ball of clay and pushes two holes right through it. Pick the object she can now reach without cutting or gluing.
quiz.answer: A two-handled cup
quiz.explain: Two holes through the clay give a surface of genus two. A doughnut and a one-handled mug each have a single hole and a dented ball has none, so only the two-handled cup matches. The count of holes is what deformation preserves.
choices: A doughnut with a single hole
A solid ball with a dent pressed in
A coffee mug with one handle

quiz.prompt: Stretching a rubber sheet preserves topological features and destroys metric ones. A figure eight is drawn on the sheet, which is then stretched and bent without tearing. Pick the feature that must survive.
quiz.answer: The self-crossing point
quiz.explain: Having a point where the curve meets itself survives any continuous deformation with a continuous inverse. Lengths, angles and relative sizes are metric quantities, and stretching changes all three.
choices: The equal size of the two loops
The right angle where the strands meet
The total length of the curve

quiz.prompt: On the set {a, b, c} a student proposes the family { {}, {a}, {b}, {a, b, c} } as the open sets. Decide whether that family is a topology.
quiz.answer: No, the union of {a} and {b} is missing
quiz.explain: A topology must contain arbitrary unions of its members, and {a, b} is absent. Holding the empty set and the whole set, and being closed under finite intersections, are necessary but not sufficient; closure under complements is not required at all.
choices: No, the union of {a} and {b} is missing
Yes, it holds the empty set and the whole set
No, the complement of {a} is missing
Yes, every finite intersection is present

quiz.prompt: Inside the real line with its usual topology, name one property that separates the open interval (0, 1) from the closed interval [0, 1], and back it with an explicit cover.
quiz.answer: The closed interval is compact and the open one is not: the open cover of (0, 1) by the sets (1/n, 1) for n = 2, 3, 4, ... has no finite subcover, since any finite choice leaves points near 0 uncovered.
quiz.explain: Compactness is the property at issue, and the shrinking cover exhibits the failure directly; Heine-Borel confirms that a closed bounded interval is compact.

quiz.prompt: Give the real line the topology whose open sets are the empty set together with the complements of finite sets, then decide whether the space is Hausdorff.
quiz.answer: No: any two nonempty open sets meet
choices: Yes, because it is really a metric space
Yes, since points can be separated by cofinite sets
No: single points fail to be closed here
No: any two nonempty open sets meet
quiz.explain: Two cofinite sets have cofinite intersection, so they cannot be disjoint. The space is T1, since points are closed, but it is not Hausdorff.

quiz.prompt: A continuous bijection runs from a compact space to a Hausdorff space. State what more can be said about it.
quiz.answer: It is a homeomorphism
choices: It is a homeomorphism only when both spaces are metric
Its inverse may still be discontinuous
It is an open map but need not be a closed one
quiz.explain: Closed subsets of a compact space are compact, and compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed, so the map carries closed sets to closed sets and its inverse is continuous. No metric hypothesis is needed, and the map turns out to be both open and closed.

quiz.prompt: A map f from X onto Y is continuous, X is compact and connected, and Y is Hausdorff. A student concludes that Y must be homeomorphic to X. Diagnose the error.
quiz.answer: f need not be injective, so Y can be a proper quotient of X
choices: f need not be injective, so Y can be a proper quotient of X
Y could fail to be compact, because surjections lose compactness
The inverse of f fails to be continuous unless Y is metrizable
Y could fail to be connected under such a map
quiz.explain: Compactness and connectedness do transfer to Y, but without injectivity there is no inverse at all. The circle is a continuous Hausdorff image of the interval, yet the two are not homeomorphic.

quiz.prompt: Take the plane set consisting of the graph of sin(1/x) for x in (0, 1] together with the segment from (0, -1) to (0, 1). Predict which pair of properties it has.
quiz.answer: Connected but not path-connected
quiz.explain: The topologist's sine curve is connected because the segment lies in the closure of the graph, yet no path reaches the segment from the oscillating branch. Path-connectedness is strictly stronger than connectedness.

quiz.prompt: Compute the Euler characteristic of a closed orientable surface of genus three.
quiz.explain: For a closed orientable surface the formula is 2 minus twice the genus, so genus three gives 2 - 6 = -4. The Euler characteristic is a homeomorphism invariant and so distinguishes the genera.

quiz.prompt: A student asserts that any continuous bijection has a continuous inverse. Supply an explicit counterexample and name the hypothesis that repairs the claim.
quiz.answer: Map the half-open interval from 0 up to 2 pi onto the unit circle by t going to (cos t, sin t). This is a continuous bijection, but the inverse jumps as a point crosses (1, 0), so it is not continuous. If the domain is compact and the codomain Hausdorff, the inverse is automatically continuous.
quiz.explain: Continuity of the inverse is an extra condition in general; compactness of the domain plus a Hausdorff target is the standard hypothesis that supplies it for free.

lesson_media.alt: A marked loop survives stretching of a gridded surface, while sphere, torus and double torus show increasing genus.
lesson_media.caption: Homeomorphisms preserve topological structure, not lengths or angles. Genus is one invariant, not a complete test in every setting.

nodes.title: Differential Geometry
nodes.goal: Curvature made precise: the mathematics behind general relativity.

quiz.prompt: A manifold is a space that looks locally like flat Euclidean space, even though it may be curved or twisted globally — a sphere's surface is the classic example. Explain why a single flat coordinate chart cannot cover the entire sphere without some kind of failure.
quiz.answer: Any single chart must omit at least one point, or distort/duplicate coordinates there
quiz.explain: This is a consequence of the sphere's global topology (its Euler characteristic and lack of a nonvanishing tangent vector field), not a failure of cleverness in choosing coordinates: no continuous, one-to-one flat coordinate map can cover the whole sphere (stereographic projection, the standard trick, always misses one point). This is exactly why manifolds are built from an ATLAS of overlapping charts rather than one global map, and why map projections of the Earth always distort or cut somewhere.
choices: Any single chart must omit at least one point, or distort/duplicate coordinates there
It cannot be done only because the sphere has finite area
A single chart works fine; this is a common misconception
It fails only for spheres, not for other curved surfaces

quiz.prompt: Gaussian curvature is an INTRINSIC property of a surface — measurable by a two-dimensional being confined to the surface, without reference to any embedding in 3-D space. A flat sheet of paper is rolled into a cylinder without stretching or tearing it. Predict what happens to its Gaussian curvature.
quiz.answer: It stays exactly zero — rolling is an isometry, and curvature is intrinsic
quiz.explain: Rolling a flat sheet into a cylinder changes its extrinsic shape (how it sits in 3-D space) but preserves all distances measured along the surface — it is an isometry. Gauss's Theorema Egregium proves Gaussian curvature depends only on those intrinsic distances, so it cannot change under an isometry. A cylinder is 'flat' in exactly this intrinsic sense, even though it looks curved from outside — which is why you can roll paper into a tube but never flatten a basketball without tearing it.
choices: It stays exactly zero — rolling is an isometry, and curvature is intrinsic
It becomes positive, matching the visible curve of the cylinder
It becomes negative, since the surface now bends away from itself
It depends on the cylinder's radius: smaller radius means more curvature

quiz.prompt: Explain what parallel transport around a closed loop on a curved surface reveals about that surface's curvature, using the example of transporting a vector around a triangle drawn on a sphere with three right angles (an octant).
quiz.answer: Parallel transport moves a vector along a path while keeping it as 'straight' as the curved surface allows at each step, with no external rotation applied. On a flat surface, transporting a vector around any closed loop and back to the start returns it to its original direction. On a curved surface it generally does not: transporting a vector around the right-angle spherical triangle rotates it by 90 degrees relative to its start, even though it was never deliberately turned. That rotation, called holonomy, is a direct, measurable signature of curvature enclosed by the loop — the bigger the enclosed curvature, the bigger the rotation.
quiz.explain: Holonomy around infinitesimal loops is literally how curvature is defined in the general (non-Gaussian) theory, and this exact idea — that transporting a vector around a closed path can rotate it — is the geometric heart of general relativity's account of gravity as spacetime curvature.

quiz.prompt: A geodesic is the curved-space generalization of a straight line: the locally shortest path between nearby points. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are great circles. A physicist claims a free-falling object in general relativity follows a geodesic of curved SPACETIME, not a curved trajectory caused by a 'force' of gravity. Interpret what this claim is asserting.
quiz.answer: Gravity is reinterpreted as spacetime curvature; falling objects move as 'straight' as the geometry allows
quiz.explain: This is the central conceptual move of general relativity: instead of gravity being a force that bends an object's path through flat space, mass and energy curve spacetime itself, and free-falling objects simply follow geodesics — the 'straightest possible' paths — through that curved geometry. What looks like acceleration due to a gravitational force is, in this picture, just an object moving inertially through curved spacetime; the apparent force is a byproduct of trying to describe curved motion using flat coordinates.
choices: Gravity is reinterpreted as spacetime curvature; falling objects move as 'straight' as the geometry allows
The claim is simply false; general relativity still treats gravity as a Newtonian force
Geodesics only apply to light rays, not massive falling objects
This describes special relativity, not general relativity
